title: Bolivian Attorney General Was Arrested After Investigating Trump-Aligned Operative
author: José Luis Granados Ceja
content:
_This article by[José Luis Granados Ceja](https://substack.com/@granadosceja)
originally appeared in the [October 29, 2026 edition of Drop Site
News](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/bolivia-attorney-general-arrest-fernando-
cerimedo), an independent, reader-funded news outlet._

The day after Bolivian Attorney General Roger Mariaca was arrested in late
September on drug-trafficking charges, presidential spokesperson José Luis
Gálvez called a press conference to thank U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio
for his support. Then he delivered a warning.

“This has only just begun,” said Gálvez.

Since then Bolivian authorities have moved to
[silence](https://x.com/AndeanInfoNet/status/2108547367809036336) a leftist
news outlet, [jailed](https://www.latintimes.com/bolivia-jails-opposition-
lawmaker-six-months-over-calls-execute-political-enemies-600375) an opposition
lawmaker on terrorism charges, and announced an
[investigation](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/12/bolivia-
investigates-ex-president-evo-morales-2009-killings) into former President Evo
Morales.

Before his arrest Mariaca had been investigating Fernando Cerimedo, the MAGA-
affiliated Argentine political operative after allegedly hiring a hitman to
kill his pregnant ex-girlfriend, Nadia Beller. Cerimedo, who was a [top
aide](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/fernando-cerimedo-rodrigo-paz-trump-
rubio) of President Rodrigo Paz, was also being investigated for drug
trafficking.

Beller told Drop Site she expects to be arrested by Bolivian authorities as
soon as Friday. She said government sources had warned her that she would be
charged with failure to report Cerimedo’s drug trafficking and election
interference. She said the Ministry of Government planned to “build a case
against me to persecute me and intimidate me, and in this way exonerate
[Cerimedo], dismiss all charges against him and absolve him of all
responsibility.”

Mariaca’s ouster sidelines a figure who had become a political problem for the
Paz government, and serves as an example of how the selective prosecution of
individuals accused of links to organized crime works to advance U.S.
interests in the region.

![Nadia Beller in a bulletproof vest escorted by Bolivian
police](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/02-nadia-
beller-escort.jpg)Bolivian activist Nadia Beller wears a bulletproof vest as
Bolivian police escort her to testify as a witness, in Santa Cruz, Bolivia,
September 23, 2026. REUTERS/Ipa Ibanez.

On September 28, **two days before Mariaca’s arrest, the United States**
[sanctioned](https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-
spokesman/2026/09/visa-restrictions-for-foreign-nationals-undermining-
democratically-elected-governments-in-western-hemisphere-countries) him and
revoked his visa for “involvement in significant corruption,” including
allegedly “soliciting and accepting bribes to facilitate narcotrafficking,”
helping “violent criminals evade justice,” and “undermining” Bolivia’s
democratic institutions.

“I think it is important that if crimes have been committed they must be
investigated and sanctioned, but his arrest, as it has happened, ignores all
legal procedures and guarantees of due process,” Canela Crespo, a Bolivian
lawyer and political analyst, told Drop Site.

Gálvez later told CNN in an October 6 interview that the timing of Mariaca’s
arrest was merely a “coincidence” and that the investigation had been ongoing
since the March arrest of Uruguayan drug trafficker Sebastián Marset.

The charges against Mariaca center on his association with Marset, whom the
former attorney general is accused of protecting through high-level bribes and
leaked intelligence. On the night of his arrest, an ambulance attempting to
leave Mariaca’s residence was stopped with **approximately $300,000** , in
both the local currency and U.S. dollars, and prosecutors claim they have
financial intelligence linking him to drug trafficking networks.

Prior to his arrest, Mariaca vehemently denied U.S. allegations regarding ties
to drug trafficking and claimed they were driven by political interests linked
to his ongoing investigations.

![Fernando Cerimedo with Donald Trump Jr. and Brad
Parscale](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/03-cerimedo-
trump-jr-parscale.jpg)Fernando Cerimedo (center left) is shown with Donald
Trump Jr. (center right) and Brad Parscale (right), former campaign manager
for President Donald Trump, in an undated photo posted to Nadia Beller’s
Facebook page in September.

Beller, who has spoken out publicly about her former partner’s political
activities throughout the region, told Drop Site that she believed the Trump
administration was involved in the decision to arrest Mariaca due to his
investigation into Cerimedo, who had ties to U.S. political figures such as
Brad Parscale and Donald Trump Jr. In September, shortly before Mariaca’s
arrest, she posted a photo of Cerimedo, Trump Jr., and Parscale to her
Facebook page.

Bolivian Vice President Edmand Lara Montaño—who has publicly broken with
Paz—leaked audio that allegedly captures Cerimedo negotiating payments for
aircraft linked to drug trafficking operations.

Beller alleges that the Paz government acted over concerns that Mariaca’s
investigation could potentially reach the highest levels, including government
ministers and even Paz’s wife, María Elena Urquidi.

Following Cerimedo’s arrest, Lara’s legal team accused Urquidi of involvement
in drug trafficking offenses, but prosecutors eventually opted to exclude her
from their investigation.

Beller accused Bolivian government authorities of deliberately stalling and
derailing the investigation into the assassination plot after her scheduled
testimony as a protected witness was abruptly suspended.

“They want to protect their allies, there is no other explanation,” Beller
told Drop Site.

Crespo said the arrest of Mariaca is not only linked to an effort to impede
investigations into Cerimedo’s alleged criminal activities but to gain control
over the country’s prosecutor’s office.

> U.S. interference and the actions of the Rodrigo Paz government seek first
> to deconstruct the judicial system as it is and to put their own pawns. What
> you have to ask is what power structure is being disassembled, and above
> all, what power structure intends to be installed in its place.
>
> Canela Crespo, Bolivian lawyer and political analyst

![Former Bolivian Attorney General Roger
Mariaca](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/04-roger-
mariaca.jpg)Bolivian Attorney General Roger Mariaca is shown in an undated
file photo. Mariaca was arrested September 30, two days after the United
States revoked their visas and accused Mariaca of corruption and aiding drug
traffickers. REUTERS.

Mariaca, appointed in 2024 during the tenure of former president Luis Arce,
had investigated politicians across the political spectrum, including
supporters of Evo Morales, Paz’s political rivals.

Kathryn Ledebur, director of the Andean Information Network and an expert on
Bolivian politics, told Drop Site that Mariaca had become a “problem” for the
Paz government.

“He had been useful for a certain amount of time, but his arrest and
prosecution of Fernando Cerimedo was very uncomfortable,” said Ledebur.

Bolivia’s Plurinational Legislative Assembly moved quickly to select Mariaca’s
replacement, naming José Armando Urioste as acting attorney general. Urioste
is behind the push to prosecute Morales and former Vice President Álvaro
García Linera over the deaths of three European citizens at the hands of
police in 2009.

Mariaca’s investigation into Cerimedo, who worked closely with the president,
threatened to further destabilize an already weakened government that had been
rocked by corruption allegations and intense protests in June and July over
Paz’s neoliberal economic policies.

Ledebur told Drop Site that in addition to worries about what Mariaca’s
investigation could reveal about high-level connections to drug trafficking,
the Paz government was also motivated by their desire to secure stability
ahead of a politically volatile time in Bolivia.

“They’ve illegally extended a state of emergency that limits freedoms
guaranteed by the constitution, and we’re at a point in time where they’d need
to push through some major legislation that could significantly affect land
tenure rights, indigenous rights, and all sorts of guarantees that were
provided in the 2009 constitution,” said Ledebur.

Social unrest in Bolivia tends to pick up in late October, after the planting
season, when highly organized indigenous communities can turn their attention
to their social demands, Ledebur explained.

The ouster of Mariaca and the derailment of his investigation into sensitive
topics gives the Paz government room to operate as it attempts to push through
unpopular reforms.

“I think what we’re seeing is they’re cleaning house to have a judiciary that
responds to their interests and their needs, and to make sure that when gross
human rights violations occur, when these violations of due process and the
Constitution continue, that there is nothing in the judicial branch that would
impede those actions or slow down this process that they seem to have planned
in advance,” Ledebur told Drop Site.

## Selective Prosecutions

Following Mariaca’s arrest, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Deputy
Secretary of State Christopher Landau issued statements of support. **A total
of 15 countries** that form part of President Donald Trump’s Shield of the
Americas initiative also [issued](https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-
the-spokesman/2026/10/joint-statement-in-support-of-bolivias-efforts-to-fight-
corruption-and-narco-trafficking) a joint statement affirming their solidarity
with Bolivia following the arrest of Mariaca.

The U.S.-led Shield of the Americas was launched in March, 2026 to coordinate
counternarcotics activities in the region and has quickly evolved into a
political alliance of countries allied with the U.S. agenda.

Since Trump’s return to office, U.S. policy in the region has been largely
dictated by the stated U.S. interest in combating “narco-terrorism.” The
kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro was justified as a “law
enforcement operation” in connection to a drug-trafficking indictment.

Yet the Trump administration has also sought closer ties to regional leaders
who face credible allegations of ties to drug trafficking. As part of his
efforts to help secure a win for the right-wing National Party in Honduras,
**Trump pardoned former President Juan Orlando Hernández** after he was
convicted by a New York court of trafficking drugs into the U.S. And Ecuador’s
President Daniel Noboa, whose family shipping business has been used by Balkan
drug traffickers to [transport cocaine](https://www.occrp.org/en/project/the-
crime-messenger/cocaine-and-bananas-how-balkan-traffickers-used-fruit-
shipments-from-the-ecuadorian-presidents-family-firm-to-smuggle-drugs), has
emerged as one of Washington’s closest allies. Noboa has used the fight
against organized crime to justify a state of exception in his country and
used this narrative to pursue his political opponents, including former
presidential candidate Luisa González, who was recently jailed.

Crespo said the Paz government’s embrace of Washington’s drug trafficking
narrative also serves similar ends.

“In the Bolivian case, very clearly, very evidently, it points to the
leadership of Evo Morales, but not only his, but also that of social leaders,
indigenous peasant leaders, and the political persecution against those of
these leaders is based on this narrative of the presence of drug trafficking,”
Crespo told Drop Site.

Benjamin Fogel, deputy director of the Alameda Institute, told Drop Site that
the U.S. strategy of using the fight against drug trafficking to advance U.S.
interests in Latin America has deep historical roots.

“This has been the pattern since [the Nixon administration] in Latin America:
selective prosecution, selective use of threats, and selective application of
ever-expanding laws to stop the threat of drug trafficking has been a means to
manipulate, intimidate, and in effect, intimidate various governments and
protect interest of the United States and its allies,” Fogel told Drop Site.

Since his election earlier this year, Colombia’s Abelardo de la Espriella, who
once [served as
lawyer](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/25/world/americas/colombia-president-
de-la-espriella-trump-us-investigation.html) for notorious Colombian
paramilitary leaders and drug traffickers, has sought to strengthen his
country’s ties to Washington and invited U.S. troops into the country to
directly participate in operations, a move that Fogel says would run afoul of
the Colombian constitution.

Fogel points out that the U.S. strategy of selective application of counter-
narcotics strategy has significant limitations, especially in the case of
countries with greater state capacity like Mexico and Brazil.

In the case of Mexico, where President Claudia Sheinbaum has refused to accept
U.S. operations, former Chihuahua Attorney General Cesar Jáuregui has been
**charged with treason for illegally permitting CIA agents to participate in
an operation**.

Most recently, the U.S. extended a visa to former Brazilian presidential
candidate Flavio Bolsonaro to allow his entry into the country after he fled
Brazil to avoid a money-laundering investigation.

“This is security slop. None of these policies are actually coherent,” said
Fogel.

_Joseph Bouchard and Camila Lourdes Galarza contributed to this report._

_Correction: A previous version of this article referred to failed Brazilian
presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro by his father’s name, Jair._
